paragraphs.heading: A virus that writes itself in
paragraphs.text: A retrovirus carries its genes as RNA, but once it gets inside a cell it turns that RNA into a DNA copy and slips the copy into the cell's own DNA. From then on the cell's genome has been changed. The virus brings its own enzyme, reverse transcriptase, to make DNA from RNA. That runs opposite to the normal direction, and the backward step is where the name retro comes from.

paragraphs.heading: From guest to provirus
paragraphs.text: Another enzyme, called integrase, stitches the new DNA into the host's genome. Once built in, the viral DNA is called a provirus. The cell now handles it like any of its own genes, reading the viral genes and making their proteins alongside its own. Those proteins are the parts needed to put together fresh copies of the virus.

paragraphs.heading: What a particle looks like
paragraphs.text: A single free retrovirus particle, or virion, is about 100 nanometres wide and wrapped in an envelope. The envelope is fatty membrane taken from the host cell as the virus buds out, studded with glycoprotein made from the virus's env gene. Inside sit two matching single strands of RNA, each 7 to 10 kilobases long. The two strands pair up with each other at matching stretches, forming a linked pair called a dimer.

paragraphs.heading: The working proteins
paragraphs.text: Gag proteins are major building blocks of the viral capsid, with roughly 2,000 to 4,000 copies in each virion, and they recognise and pack the viral RNA into new particles. Pol proteins make the viral DNA and fit it into the host's DNA after infection. Env proteins let the virus attach to and enter a cell. One part of Env grips particular receptors on the cell surface, and another part, anchored in the membrane, fuses the virus with the cell, which is why Env is what makes a retrovirus infectious.

paragraphs.heading: Disease and harmless kin
paragraphs.text: Many retroviruses cause serious illness in people, other mammals and birds. Some cause cancer: human T-lymphotropic virus, or HTLV, causes a type of leukaemia in people, and murine leukaemia viruses do the same in mice. The lentiviruses, or slow viruses, include HIV-1 and HIV-2, which cause AIDS in humans. Yet the spumaviruses, or foamy viruses, are harmless and have no link to any disease in people or animals.

paragraphs.heading: An ancient guest, a modern tool
paragraphs.text: Some animal genomes carry inherited provirus DNA, known as endogenous retroviruses. That evidence suggests vertebrates have been infected by retroviruses for at least 450 million years. Their skill at inserting DNA into a cell has also made them useful in the laboratory. Molecular biologists use them as research tools, and they have worked well as systems for delivering genes into cells.
